Illinois enters the 2026 NCAA Tournament at 24-7 overall and 15-5 in the Big Ten after closing the regular season with a 78-72 road win at Maryland on March 8, 2026. That win explicitly locked up a top-four Big Ten seed and followed an 80-54 home win over Oregon on March 3, leaving the Illini with one of the league’s best résumés entering March. ([fightingillini.com](https://fightingillini.com/news/2026/3/8/mens-basketball-11-illinois-outlasts-maryland-secures-quarterfinal-berth-in-b1g-tourney.aspx?utm_source=openai))

Offensively, this is a modern Brad Underwood team built on volume threes, offensive rebounding, and frontcourt skill. Illinois averaged 85.5 points per game through 20 games in official midseason team notes, hit 11.1 threes per game, attempted 31.1 threes per game, and posted a +11.2 rebounding margin; by March 7, Illinois’ own game notes said the Illini led the nation in adjusted offensive efficiency at 131.8 and that the rating would be the best of the KenPom era if maintained. The specific on-court profile backs that up: Illinois had 22 games with 10+ made threes by March 3, including 15 made threes in the January 21 win over Maryland, their most in a Big Ten home game since March 3, 2005. Their common offensive actions are spread pick-and-pop and five-out spacing through Tomislav Ivisic and David Mirkovic, with Keaton Wagler and Andrej Stojakovic attacking second-side gaps. In the December 6 win over Tennessee, Illinois changed the game with a 10-3 run out of halftime capped by two Wagler threes, a clear example of Underwood leaning into quick-hitting perimeter actions after the break. In the January 21 win over Maryland, Illinois closed the first half on a 28-6 run, driven by shot-making and ball movement, with Wagler posting 13 points and eight assists in Boswell’s absence. ([gohuskies.com](https://gohuskies.com/documents/download/2026/1/28/2025-26_MBB_Opponent_Game_Notes_Game_21_Illinois.pdf))

The personnel tells you how the scheme functions. Keaton Wagler is the primary engine: 17.9 points, 4.8 rebounds, and 4.4 assists per game over 32 games, plus 74 made threes at 40.2%. He plays like a lead wing creator rather than a pure guard. His specific takeover moments matter: he scored 46 points at Purdue on January 24, 2026, according to Illinois-linked season records, had 34 in the February 10 overtime loss to Wisconsin, and scored 23 in the February 27 loss to Michigan. He also had a 19-point, 10-assist double-double in the December 13 loss to Nebraska. Andrej Stojakovic gives them a true shot-making wing: 13.4 points per game, 49.1% from the field, 83.0% at the line. He went for 23 on 11-of-16 shooting against Texas Tech on November 11, 30 against Maryland on January 21, and 21 points with 12 rebounds against Oregon on March 3. David Mirkovic has been their interior scorer and glass-cleaner at 13.4 points and a team-best 7.8 rebounds per game; his 22-point, 11-rebound line at Maryland on March 8 is the exact template for his value in tournament basketball. Tomislav Ivisic spaces the floor as a trail big and pick-and-pop five: 10.0 points, 5.5 rebounds, 1.6 assists, and 43 made threes. Kylan Boswell, although only at 25 games, gave them 13.2 points and 3.3 assists per game and remains the steadiest traditional organizer when available. ([fightingillini.com](https://fightingillini.com/sports/mens-basketball/stats/2025-26))

Defensively, Illinois is not built around turnover pressure. Through 20 games they averaged only 3.7 steals while opponents averaged 6.1, but they held teams to 40.4% shooting overall and 31.6% from three, while blocking 5.0 shots per game and dominating the glass at 41.6 rebounds per game. That points to a containment-and-rebound philosophy: protect the paint with length, stay out of foul trouble when possible, and finish possessions. Zvonimir Ivisic is the central rim-protection piece at 2.1 blocks per game, while Tomislav Ivisic adds 0.6. When Illinois locks in, the defense looks imposing. Against Oregon on March 3, the Illini held the Ducks to 1-for-16 shooting during a 24-2 run, then later held them without a field goal for 7:38 during a 23-6 surge. Against Maryland on January 21, Illinois shut down the Terps with a 28-6 run to end the first half. The weakness is that elite offenses with shot-makers can pull the bigs into space and force long defensive possessions; Michigan scored 84 on February 27, Nebraska shot 51.6% in its 83-80 win on December 13, and Wisconsin got 92 in overtime on February 10. ([gohuskies.com](https://gohuskies.com/documents/download/2026/1/28/2025-26_MBB_Opponent_Game_Notes_Game_21_Illinois.pdf))

Underwood’s coaching philosophy remains aggressive and matchup-driven. He schedules hard, and Illinois’ official notes highlighted marquee nonconference games against Texas Tech, Alabama, UConn, Tennessee, and Missouri as part of that philosophy. In-game, he has shown a clear willingness to alter emphasis. The Tennessee game is the cleanest example: after managing only one field goal in the final three minutes of the first half, Illinois came out of halftime with that 10-3 run and re-centered the offense on Wagler’s perimeter shooting. The Maryland home game is another: without Boswell, Illinois redistributed creation to Wagler, who delivered eight assists, while Stojakovic became the first-option scorer and Illinois exploded late in the half. The flip side is that Underwood teams can be vulnerable late when the shot profile dries up or the opponent attacks their bigs in space. Michigan State erased a nine-point second-half deficit on February 7 and won 85-82 in overtime after taking its first second-half lead with 32 seconds left. Wisconsin beat Illinois 92-90 in overtime three days later despite Wagler’s 34 and Tomislav Ivisic’s 19-and-11, a sign that the defensive counters were not enough once the game got scrambled. ([scarletknights.com](https://scarletknights.com/documents/download/2026/1/7/ILLINI_MBB_G15_Notes-Rutgers_1-8-26.pdf))

Clutch execution has therefore been mixed, and the named games matter. Positive examples: Illinois beat Texas Tech 81-77 on November 11, with Stojakovic blocking a would-be game-tying three with nine seconds left. Illinois beat Tennessee 75-62 on December 6 after seizing control with the early second-half 10-3 burst. Illinois also won at Maryland 78-72 on March 8 in a back-and-forth game, with Mirkovic posting 22 and 11 in what Illinois called a clutch double-double. Negative examples: Nebraska hit a last-second three to beat Illinois 83-80 on December 13 despite Wagler’s 19-point, 10-assist game. Michigan State rallied and beat Illinois 85-82 in overtime on February 7 after Illinois had led by nine in the second half. Wisconsin then beat them 92-90 in overtime on February 10. Those three losses reveal the pressure points: late-clock defense, transition matchups after misses, and half-court scoring when the first option is taken away. ([fightingillini.com](https://fightingillini.com/news/2025/11/12/mens-basketball-14-illinois-secures-first-ranked-win-with-thrilling-victory-over-11-texas-tech.aspx))

The notable wins are tournament-caliber and revealing. Texas Tech (81-77, Nov. 11) showed Illinois could close a ranked game with wing shot-making and a defensive play at the horn. Tennessee (75-62, Dec. 6) showed physical toughness and halftime adjustment capacity on a neutral floor. At Purdue (88-82, Jan. 24), Illinois proved its offense travels against elite competition; that game also featured Wagler’s 46-point eruption. Maryland at home (89-70, Jan. 21) showed ceiling performance without Boswell, while Maryland on the road (78-72, Mar. 8) showed mature closeout ability. The worst losses also tell the truth: Nebraska’s 83-80 win in Champaign exposed perimeter containment and end-game communication; Michigan’s 84-70 win on February 27 showed that a top-tier opponent can survive Illinois’ early punch, then wear down its defense; Wisconsin’s 92-90 overtime win showed how thin the margin becomes when Underwood’s group cannot get enough stops late. ([fightingillini.com](https://fightingillini.com/news/2025/11/12/mens-basketball-14-illinois-secures-first-ranked-win-with-thrilling-victory-over-11-texas-tech.aspx))

As for Underwood’s NCAA tournament history, he reached the Round of 64 at Stephen F. Austin in 2014 and the Round of 32 in 2016 at Oklahoma State. At Illinois, he reached the Round of 32 in 2021, the Round of 64 in 2022 and 2023, the Elite Eight in 2024, and the Round of 32 in 2025 after beating Xavier and losing to Kentucky. That matters because this 2026 team resembles his best Illinois teams offensively, but with more volatility late. The scouting takeaway is simple: Illinois can overwhelm opponents with spacing, shooting, and second-shot volume, but if a tournament game becomes a one-possession defensive execution contest in the last two minutes, there is enough 2025-26 evidence to think the Illini are dangerous but not fully dependable. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025%E2%80%9326_Illinois_Fighting_Illini_men%27s_basketball_team))
forecaster:
Illinois enters the 2026 NCAA Tournament as one of the strongest two-way profiles in the country, and the statistical case is more convincing than the casual narrative might suggest. Through games in early to mid-March 2026, Illinois is 24-7 overall and finished 15-5 in the Big Ten, with a Sports-Reference Simple Rating System (SRS) of 27.01 and strength of schedule of 11.88, which ranks 17th nationally on that site. WarrenNolan’s comparison board places Illinois 5th in NET, 14th in KPI, 15th in SOR, 12th in WAB, 11th in Sagarin, with an average composite placement of 11.4; that same comparison page lists Illinois 6th in ESPN BPI and 5th in NET as of March 10, 2026. NCAA’s published NET rankings also had Illinois 5th through games of February 27, 2026, with an excellent 8-6 record in Quadrant 1 and 6-1 in Quadrant 2, which is a resume profile consistent with a protected seed. ([sports-reference.com](https://www.sports-reference.com/cbb/schools/illinois/men/2026.html?utm_source=openai))

The headline number is the offense. Sports-Reference lists Illinois with a 125.8 offensive rating, the best mark in Division I, while allowing 103.2 per 100 possessions defensively. TeamRankings, using its own efficiency framework later in the season, shows Illinois around 1.232 to 1.240 points per possession on offense and roughly 0.997 to 1.019 allowed on defense, depending on update date; translated to per-100-possession language, that is about 123.2 to 124.0 offensively and 99.7 to 101.9 defensively. That is not just “good offense, decent defense”; it is elite offense paired with defense that is comfortably tournament-caliber. The likely takeaway is that Illinois has been tracked a bit differently by source, but the shared conclusion is stable: this is a top-tier offense with a defense that grades much better than the stereotype of a run-and-gun Big Ten scoring team. ([sports-reference.com](https://www.sports-reference.com/cbb/schools/illinois/men/2026.html?utm_source=openai))

In stylistic terms, Illinois is built on shot quality, spacing, and extra possessions. TeamRankings shows an offensive effective field goal percentage between 55.1% and 55.5%, turnover rate between 11.1% and 11.5%, offensive rebound rate between 38.4% and 38.8%, and free-throw rate between 0.329 and 0.343 FTA/FGA. Its 3-point attempt rate sits at 50.7% to 51.2%, meaning just over half of Illinois’s field-goal attempts come from three. That is a massive volume indicator, but it is not empty bombing: Illinois is also finishing 58.2% on twos and 34.7% from three in the late-season TeamRankings snapshot. The core offensive identity is therefore clear: high-volume threes, excellent ball security, and ferocious work on the offensive glass. Teams usually get two of those three; Illinois gets all three. ([teamrankings.com](https://www.teamrankings.com/ncaa-basketball/matchup/fighting-illini-terrapins-2026-03-08/efficiency))

The defensive profile is subtler and probably where the numbers diverge most from conventional wisdom. Illinois is not especially disruptive in forcing turnovers; opponents are coughing it up on only about 10.0% to 10.1% of plays, which is low-pressure by elite-defense standards. But Illinois compensates by winning the more stable defensive factors: opponent eFG% is just 46.7% to 47.6%, defensive rebounding is 74.1% to 74.6%, and opponent free-throw rate is only 0.188 to 0.206 FTA/FGA. Opponents are shooting just 48.0% on twos and 31.4% from three in one late-season snapshot. So the Illini defense is not chaos-driven; it is suppression-driven. They contest shots, finish possessions, and avoid fouling. That tends to scale better in March than defenses that rely heavily on live-ball turnover variance. ([teamrankings.com](https://www.teamrankings.com/ncaa-basketball/matchup/fighting-illini-terrapins-2026-03-08/efficiency?utm_source=openai))

Pace is the one area where public perception may be a bit off. Because Illinois scores 84.3 points per game and plays aesthetically open basketball, the eye test can make them feel extremely fast. But the possession data suggests more of an upper-middle tempo than true track meet. TeamRankings has Illinois at about 68.1 to 68.5 possessions per game in late-season snapshots. That is quick enough to stress opponents, but not so fast that the team becomes structurally reckless. In other words, Illinois is producing huge raw scoring volume more because of efficiency than because of sheer pace inflation. That distinction matters for tournament forecasting, because highly efficient teams with only moderately elevated tempo tend to be more resilient than teams whose numbers are pace-created. ([teamrankings.com](https://www.teamrankings.com/ncaa-basketball/matchup/fighting-illini-terrapins-2026-03-08/efficiency))

On strength of schedule, the profile is unquestionably battle-tested. Sports-Reference puts Illinois’s SOS at 11.88, 17th nationally. TeamRankings rates Illinois’s past schedule strength at 14.1, 7th nationally, while WarrenNolan lists Illinois 19th in NET SOS and 39th in non-conference SOS. Those measures are not identical, but together they tell a consistent story: Illinois has not inflated its profile against soft competition. It has played a demanding schedule, especially once conference play is accounted for, and still maintained top-tier efficiency margins. ([sports-reference.com](https://www.sports-reference.com/cbb/schools/illinois/men/2026.html?utm_source=openai))

Recent form is also strong. TeamRankings lists Illinois 6th nationally in its “Last 10 Games” predictive rating at 25.1, slightly stronger than its full-season predictive rating of 23.2, which ranks 8th. That implies Illinois was playing a bit better entering March than its already elite full-season baseline. TeamRankings also rates the Illini 6th in away games, 8th in neutral games, 7th in conference games, and 2nd nationally in first-half performance. That first-half marker is especially notable: Illinois has tended to seize control early rather than merely outlasting teams late, a trait associated with matchup clarity and translatable preparation edges. ([teamrankings.com](https://www.teamrankings.com/ncaa-basketball/matchup/fighting-illini-terrapins-2026-03-08/power-ratings?utm_source=openai))

The eye-test divergence is this: Illinois may still be discussed as an offense-first team that can be vulnerable if the jumpers cool off. The data only partially supports that. Yes, the offense is three-heavy, with a 3-point attempt rate above 50%. But Illinois is not dependent on low-probability shotmaking alone. Its turnover avoidance is elite, its offensive rebounding is elite, and its free-throw generation is solid. On the other side, it does not need steals to defend well because it closes possessions with rebounds and keeps opponents off the line. If there is a real statistical vulnerability, it is probably that the defense does not manufacture many turnovers, so opponents can usually get shots up; against an elite shot-making offense, that reduces Illinois’s margin for error. But the broader evidence says the Illini are much more complete than the stereotype. ([teamrankings.com](https://www.teamrankings.com/ncaa-basketball/matchup/fighting-illini-terrapins-2026-03-08/efficiency))

Bottom line: Illinois’s 2026 tournament profile is that of a genuine national-contender offense backed by a quietly excellent, low-foul, shot-suppressing defense. The resume metrics say top-5 NET and top-10ish composite quality; the predictive metrics say top-10 nationally, including No. 6 in BPI; the raw team data says No. 1 offense by Sports-Reference and a defense strong enough to sustain deep-run viability. If you are building a quantitative forecast, Illinois should be treated as a high-upside contender whose underlying efficiency profile is stronger and more balanced than the public shorthand implies. ([warrennolan.com](https://www.warrennolan.com/basketball/2026/compare-rankings?utm_source=openai))
matchup-analyst:
Illinois is built to score efficiently in the half court without playing fast. Through games played March 8, 2026, TeamRankings lists the Illini at 84.5 points per game, 1.240 points per possession, 55.5% effective field goal rate, only 11.5% turnovers per play, and 38.8% offensive-rebound rate, while playing just 68.1 possessions per game. That profile says their preferred game is not chaos; it is a controlled efficiency game where they get a shot, crash size to the glass, and avoid giveaways. Illinois’ own game notes also describe them as a top-15 KenPom offense for the third straight season, and by early February listed them No. 5 in KenPom and “the tallest team in the nation” at 79.5 inches average height. ([teamrankings.com](https://www.teamrankings.com/ncaa-basketball/matchup/fighting-illini-terrapins-2026-03-08/efficiency?utm_source=openai))

The first disruption tactic is to make Illinois finish over length without second shots. Their offensive-rebound rate is one of the load-bearing stats in the profile, so opponents that neutralize the glass change the game. Michigan State’s 85-82 overtime win on February 7 is the cleanest example: MSU won the rebound battle 48-38, got 15 boards and 18 assists, and held Illinois to 26-of-71 shooting overall and 10-of-36 from three. Jaxon Kohler had 15 rebounds and Carson Cooper added 9; Illinois’ front line did not dominate physically despite its size. If you keep Mirkovic, Tomislav Ivisic, and Zvonimir Ivisic from turning misses into put-backs, Illinois becomes more jump-shot dependent. ([espn.com](https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/boxscore/_/gameId/401830778))

The second disruption tactic is to make Illinois win with contested perimeter creation rather than paint touches plus kick-outs. In that same Michigan State loss, Keaton Wagler scored 16 but needed 16 field-goal attempts, and Illinois shot only 37% overall. Against UConn on November 28, Illinois managed only 61 points in a 74-61 loss. Against Tennessee on December 6, Illinois won 75-62, but that was a lower-possession, more physical game, not the free-flowing scoring environment Illinois prefers. Those results point to the same formula: shrink the floor, switch size onto wings, and force long-clock offense. ([espn.com](https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/boxscore/_/gameId/401830778))

On press vulnerability, the evidence cuts two ways. The season-long numbers say Illinois is generally hard to speed up: 11.5% turnovers per play offensively is excellent, and Illinois had only seven turnovers in the March 8 win at Maryland. Indiana’s official recap of its February 15 loss noted Illinois shot 45.5% and had seven assists against just one turnover. That strongly suggests ordinary token pressure is unlikely to crack them because Boswell and Wagler can initiate and the frontcourt can pass. ([teamrankings.com](https://www.teamrankings.com/ncaa-basketball/matchup/fighting-illini-terrapins-2026-03-08/efficiency?utm_source=openai))

But defensive pressure still matters if it is attached to physical rebounding and late-clock shot contests. Michigan State forced Illinois into a worse version of itself without generating huge steal totals: Illinois had only four turnovers, yet still lost because the Spartans controlled the glass and held the Illini to 28% from three. So the right “press” plan is not gambling full-court for steals; it is disruptive pickup pressure into a loaded half-court shell. Make Boswell or Wagler initiate offense later, then keep Illinois from flowing into early drag screens and deep seals. ([espn.com](https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/boxscore/_/gameId/401830778))

Zone vulnerability is harder to prove directly because available primary sources do not publish Illinois’ exact zone-possession splits, but the shot-distribution evidence gives a practical angle. Illinois takes a lot of threes: in the Michigan State game they attempted 36 threes out of 71 shots, and at Maryland they took 24 threes out of 55 shots. When Illinois is hot, zone gets shredded; against Northwestern on February 4, the Illini hit 17 threes in an 84-44 win. When they are cold, the offense can flatten into perimeter volume; Michigan State held them to 10-of-36 from deep, and Maryland nearly beat them despite Illinois shooting only 5-of-24 from three because the game tightened and Illinois had to survive at the foul line and on the glass. So a compact matchup zone is viable only if your closeouts are clean and your defensive rebounding is elite. A soft zone that gives up rhythm catch-and-shoot looks is dead on arrival against this roster. ([espn.com](https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/boxscore/_/gameId/401830778))

Preferred pace is clearly moderate. Illinois averages roughly 68 possessions, while many power-conference track meets live above 70. To force the opposite, an underdog should avoid early-clock threes and prioritize offensive floor balance; every live-ball miss or leak-out fuels Illinois’ easiest scoring chances. Conversely, if you want to speed them up, the model is Alabama’s 90-86 win on November 19. Alabama played the game in the 90s, and Illinois’ defense was dragged into a higher-scoring exchange. Illinois can score in that environment, but the Illini are less dominant there because their defense is not built on takeaways. TeamRankings shows opponents turn it over on only 10.0% of plays against Illinois, and Sports Illustrated noted Illinois ranked 365th nationally in defensive turnover rate and 364th in steal percentage after the Indiana game. That means if you can handle their size, you can often get into your offense cleanly. ([espn.com](https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/team/schedule/_/id/356/season/2026))

Size and athleticism mismatches matter at every spot. At guard, Wagler is a 17.9-point, 4.4-assist lead option and Boswell gives them another physical initiator; small backcourts can be shot over or posted by stronger guards. On the wing, Andrej Stojakovic gives them another double-figure scorer with size. Up front, David Mirkovic leads the team at 7.8 rebounds per game, Tomislav Ivisic stretches the floor, and 7-foot-2 Zvonimir Ivisic supplies rim protection with 2.1 blocks per game. Illinois’ vulnerability is not lack of size; it is lateral quickness and stretch coverage when opponents force the bigs to defend in space. Michigan State exploited that with Jeremy Fears Jr. creating 26 points and 15 assists from the lead-guard spot while the Spartans’ front line still controlled the boards. ([espn.com](https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/team/stats/_/id/356/sort/gamesPlayed))

Isolation versus team offense percentages are the weakest public-data area from available primary sources; exact Synergy possession shares were not accessible in the searched official materials. What can be said, and should guide scouting, is that Illinois’ statistical fingerprint looks more team-offense than pure isolation: 14 assists at Maryland, 13 assists at Michigan State, low turnover rate, and multiple double-figure scorers. Yet when the offense bogs down, Wagler becomes the bailout creator. His 46-point eruption at Purdue on January 24 and 28 points at Nebraska on February 1 show Illinois can survive by individual shot-making when necessary. If you want to beat them, you must prevent the game from reaching “Wagler rescue mode” by crowding his pull-up windows and forcing the ball to non-creators late in the clock. ([espn.com](https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/boxscore/_/gameId/401825567))

Transition frequency is also not fully published in the official sources I could verify, but the defensive takeaway stats are revealing: Illinois does not force many turnovers, so its transition offense is more likely to come from rebounds than steals. That means transition defense against Illinois starts with shot selection. You cannot take reckless long jumpers that create run-outs for Boswell, Wagler, and Stojakovic. On the other end, Illinois’ transition defense can be tested because they play big and do not generate many live-ball stops. Alabama’s 90 points and Michigan State’s 85 both show that quality offensive teams can score enough before Illinois’ size gets set. ([teamrankings.com](https://www.teamrankings.com/ncaa-basketball/matchup/fighting-illini-terrapins-2026-03-08/efficiency?utm_source=openai))

Coaching adaptability under Brad Underwood is real. The clearest 2026 evidence is Illinois winning consecutive road games over No. 4 Purdue, 88-82 on January 24, and No. 5 Nebraska, 78-69 on February 1. In the Nebraska game, Illinois trailed 39-33 at halftime and flipped the second half 45-30. That is a concrete in-game adjustment example, not theory. Underwood’s staff also stabilized after early losses to Alabama and UConn; by early February Illinois had risen to No. 5 in KenPom and stacked six Quad 1 wins. ([purduesports.com](https://purduesports.com/news/2026/01/24/4-purdue-drops-second-straight-game?utm_source=openai))

Concrete gameplan: To beat Illinois you must do five things. First, win the defensive glass; Michigan State’s plus-10 rebounding margin is the template. Second, shrink the paint and live with hard-contested threes rather than post seals and second shots. Third, attack their big lineups with speed in space; Fears’ 26 points and 15 assists for Michigan State is the model. Fourth, do not rely on turnovers to save you offensively, because Illinois rarely gives the ball away; instead, disrupt timing and force late-clock jumpers. Fifth, offensively either go all the way up-tempo with confident guard play, like Alabama’s 90-point win, or all the way the other direction with a physical half-court grind that keeps Illinois off the glass. What you cannot do is play an average-possession, average-physicality game. In that middle ground, Illinois’ size, shooting, and rebounding usually overwhelm teams. ([espn.com](https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/boxscore/_/gameId/401830778))
